title: PM says it is 'clear' Russia interfered with Brexit vote
content: Andy Burnham has said Russia did interfere with the Brexit referendum and warned that similar activities were taking place in France and Germany. The prime minister told The Rest is Politics podcast that upon arriving in No 10, he had asked about possible Russian interference in the 2016 vote, adding: "I've had the clear answer that, yes, there was." "I think we've been too much on the back foot on that actually and we haven't informed people sufficiently about the extent to which people are seeking to disrupt the political process from overseas," he added. Burnham did not provide further details about the type or extent of Moscow's activity during the Brexit referendum. Britain Unbound, a pro-Brexit campaign group, said Burnham's comments were "another crude attempt to undermine the legitimacy of the decision that the British people made in 2016". It said that foreign interference in UK elections was "obviously unacceptable" but added: "There is no good reason to believe that Russian intervention influenced the outcome of the referendum in 2016. "It is also insulting to suggest that voters were so easily duped." In his interview, due to be released on Monday, Burnham said he had discussed the problem of Russian interference with Chancellor Friedrich Merz during his visit to Germany earlier this week. "There is certainly misinformation, disinformation that is emanating from Russia into German politics," he said. He continued: "These things are important now to put clearly on the record and I believe help voters in Germany and France understand that some of this politics is instigated via our enemies, namely Russia." It is the first time a UK prime minister has said Russia sought to sway the 2016 Brexit poll but there have long been warnings about efforts by the Kremlin to exert influence on UK politics. In 2020, Parliament's Intelligence and Security Committee published a report into Russian interventions in UK elections and referendums. It did not provide a definitive conclusion on whether Russia had attempted to influence the results of the EU referendum but did criticise successive governments for failing to fully assess or counter the threat. In response, the Russian foreign minister dismissed the report out of hand and called it "Russophobia". And a Kremlin spokesman said Russia did not meddle in other countries' elections. In the same year, however, the then-Conservative government said it was "almost certain that Russian actors sought to interfere" in the 2019 general election. BBC Verify has tracked Russian-linked disinformation campaigns including using AI to create fake videos which impersonate journalists and news organisations reporting on Ukraine. One fake news website falsely claimed that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky had bought a mansion owned by King Charles at a discounted price. Earlier this year, Vijay Rangarajan, head of the UK Electoral Commission, told MPs that Russian deepfake videos had been "used extensively in elections around the world". "There is no reason to assume Britain would be an exception," he added. Last month, during his speech to the United Nations, Burnham accused Russian agencies of using "every means at their disposal to spread lies and disinformation and prey on people's fears". He announced that the UK would set up a new centre to "stem the poisonous tide" of disinformation. A Downing Street spokesperson said: "We are focused on ensuring our citizens and our institutions are protected from foreign powers and their proxies seeking to threaten lives and undermine our democratic values. "We are doing this by strengthening our powers through the National Security Act, strengthening the resilience of our institutions and critical national infrastructure, strengthening our borders, and strengthening our police and intelligence agencies." Sign up for our Politics Essential newsletter to keep up with the inner workings of Westminster and beyond. Addressing the Commons, Burnham is expected to say that a new deal with the EU could help tackle illegal immigration and boost economic growth. Nigel Farage says he was "very surprised" the PM had reignited the Brexit debate. The PM says a referendum wouldn't be the right thing now but the UK needs to consider its options for the future. Andy Burnham says rejoining the EU is among options the government could look at - telling the BBC the current Brexit settlement has caused "more harm than good". A decade ago, many economists argued the UK would sustain longer-term economic damage by leaving the EU. So what did happen? Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: Australian detained in Iraq for years on his way home
content: Australian engineer Robert Pether has left Iraq five years after he was arrested and, according to the UN, arbitrarily detained. The 51-year-old was jailed on fraud charges in 2021 alongside a colleague amid a contract dispute between the consulting firm he worked for and the Central Bank of Iraq. The UN has said Pether's detention was illegal, and an international court has ruled his employer is not responsible for the business disagreement. On Monday the Australian government confirmed Pether was on his way to being reunited with his family - who feared he would die in prison - at their home in Ireland. Foreign Minister Penny Wong said the outcome followed "many years of persistent advocacy" by Australia and the Irish authorities. "I spoke to Mr Pether shortly before his departure from Baghdad and am pleased he is now free to move forward with his life," she said. "I'm hugely relieved," his wife Desree Pether told the BBC in a statement. "It's been an absolute nightmare, especially these last few months. So many obstacles and plot twists right up to the last minute." "We weren't going to say anything until he was safe at the end of his journey," she said, adding he was still in transit. Pether was conditionally released from prison in Iraq last year, but barred from leaving the country, with Canberra at the time saying he continued to face the prospect of more legal proceedings. Pether worked in the Middle East for almost a decade before taking on a huge rebuild of the Central Bank of Iraq's Baghdad headquarters in 2015. He was arrested alongside his CME Consulting colleague, Egyptian Khalid Radwan, after the bank accused the men of stealing money from the project. After being held without charge for almost six months, and then subjected to a speedy trial, the two were each given a five-year jail sentence and a joint fine of $12m (A$18.4m, £8.8m). However, a 2022 report from the UN determined that the case contravened international law, and that Pether and Khalid had been subjected to "abusive and coercive" interrogations. Iraq's government has previously denied allegations of ill treatment. In 2023, the International Chamber of Commerce's (ICC) Court of Arbitration ruled that Iraq's central bank was at fault in the dispute with CME, and ordered it to pay $13m to the company. The United Arab Emirates' attorney-general also alleges the co-pilot was trying to crash the plane into Tel Aviv's airport. Israel said in September it would act in response to UK sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank. Casualties have been reported on the vessel, identified by a maritime intelligence firm as the oil and chemical tanker, Acers. The consulate, first established in 1838, was set to be closed by the Israeli government in retaliation for UK sanctions. The ceasefire saw thousands of Palestinians held by Israel released in return for the remaining hostages held in Gaza. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: One killed, 11 injured in second Houthi strike on Riyadh airport in two days
content: One person has been killed and 11 injured in a second strike on the international airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh, officials have said. A Saudi military spokesman said a projectile had hit King Khalid International Airport on Sunday, causing a fire in one of its passenger halls. Saudi Arabia's civil aviation authority said in a statement on X that one person, a Pakistani resident, had been killed in the attack. It comes a day after a strike on the same airport killed 13 people and injured 308 others, following similar strikes earlier this week. The Houthis in Yemen said they were behind the attacks and warned airlines and passengers against using Saudi Arabian airports and airspace. The group said they had targeted the airport with a mix of ballistic and cruise missiles, as well as drones in the past 24 hours. They also attacked oil facilities and Dammam airport in eastern Saudi Arabia, their military spokesman Brig Gen Yahya Saree said. He vowed to continue the "escalating operations deep inside Saudi Arabia", warning that all Saudi airports were potential targets apart from those in the holy cities of Mecca and Medina. The Houthis have said they are targeting Saudi Arabia over its support for government forces in Yemen's civil war, as well as an air strike on the airport in Sanaa. On Sunday Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki, spokesman for the Saudi-led military coalition, said air defences had intercepted a missile near the airport in Riyadh, while authorities were dealing with the fire caused by an "unknown projectile" that hit Passenger Hall No 4. US President Donald Trump has said the US would "make a decision" and "move very quickly" on whether to strike the Houthis, while UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting suggested the UK could "potentially" provide more support for Saudi Arabia. Saturday's strike was the deadliest single attack on a Gulf Arab country since the war between Israel, the US and Iran began in February. The Saudi-led coalition vowed to respond, calling it a "war crime". Four Saudi nationals, two people from Bangladesh and one person each from the US, Jordan, Palestine, Syria, Sudan and Egypt were among the dead, the Saudi civil aviation authority said. The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia said on Sunday that an Indian man had succumbed to the injuries he sustained in the attack. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio condemned the attacks and confirmed that a US citizen was killed in the strikes. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said he was "appalled". The UK Foreign Office is advising against all travel to parts of Saudi Arabia, including areas within 10km (6.2 miles) of the border with Yemen, while other western embassies have warned their nationals about travel in the region. Houthi-run Al Masirah TV said "the Saudi enemy" had launched an air strike on Sanaa International Airport in Yemen's capital. A residential home in the city was also struck, killing a child and injuring six people, the media outlet reported. Saudi Arabia has not confirmed the attacks and the BBC has been unable to verify this report. Abdullah Al-Alimi Bawazir, vice-president of Yemen's internationally recognised government, called for "decisive actions" from regional and international partners. Riyadh's airport was struck on Thursday, an attack that killed three Saudi nationals . The Houthis claimed responsibility and said they had used cruise missiles to target the airport. There were two other deadly attacks on Saudi airports in Abha and Riyadh in the two days prior to that. The latest uptick in violence comes after a temporary ceasefire between the Houthis and Saudi-led forces, brokered in 2022, collapsed in July. The conflict worsened after the Houthis seized strategically important stretches of the Red Sea coast in a rapid offensive, prompting Saudi strikes. Yemeni pro-government forces later said they had secured the regions. The Houthis currently control around a quarter of Yemeni territory and as much as 80% of the country's population. The Iran-backed armed group hopes to eventually seize complete control. Saudi Arabia fears this would lead to the establishment of an Iranian satellite state on its southern border. Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told his Saudi Arabian counterpart on Sunday that his country was ready to provide assistance to "facilitate dialogue between Saudi Arabia and Yemen", referring to the Houthi administration. The boat was travelling from Djibouti to Yemen with 305 people on board, when it capsized near the port town of Obock on Thursday night. The Houthis have claimed responsibility for the attacks, which mark an escalation in the conflict. The families allege that men with links to the Saudi government helped those who carried out the 2001 attacks, something the country denies. The BBC reports from a school in Taiz, Yemen, where children are determined to keep learning despite the vicious civil war. Saudi-backed forces gave conflicting reports of whether they had also seized the port city of Mokha, near the Bab al-Mandab Strait. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: Documents falsified to evade tax on Abramovich's wealth
content: The world's biggest accountancy firm helped in falsifying documents to hide Roman Abramovich's wealth and evade tax, BBC Panorama has found. Accounts signed off by Deloitte in Cyprus meant assets such as superyachts, mansions and private jets worth $672m (£508m) vanished from Abramovich's company accounts. Deloitte also appears to have advised on a scheme to evade a huge tax bill on the oligarch's wealth through the falsification of documents. Barrister Andrew Mitchell KC, an expert in financial services law, said Panorama's evidence showed the scheme was "straightforward" tax evasion and "it couldn't be more blatant". Roman Abramovich's lawyers said he denies that he evaded tax or concealed his fortune. They said Panorama provided no evidence he knew about, authorised or directed the falsification of any document and said it was legitimate to rely on advice from professionals. Deloitte Cyprus said it "acts in compliance with applicable laws". The findings are being revealed following a joint investigation between BBC Panorama and the Bureau of Investigative Journalism. For nearly two decades, Roman Abramovich was the most famous Russian oligarch in the UK, welcomed in London where he bought Chelsea Football Club in 2003 and bankrolled the club's most successful period. But after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, he was sanctioned by the UK government as an associate of President Vladimir Putin and forced to sell the club. Abramovich has been reported to be living in Turkey, a safe haven for him because it did not apply sanctions. In the Channel Island of Jersey, £5.4bn of his assets remain frozen and a criminal investigation has been going on for four years. The oligarch's lawyers told the BBC he denies the allegations in the Jersey investigation and says it was "undertaken for political purposes". Our investigation has uncovered new evidence about the way Abramovich's business empire has been run. It also raises serious questions about the integrity of some of his professional advisers. The evidence is contained in a leak that includes thousands of documents about the oligarch's finances and the operations of a network of offshore companies administered from Cyprus - which used to be a tax haven popular with Russians - between 1995 and 2022. The BBC and media partners including the Guardian, Paper Trail Media, the Organised Crime and Corruption Reporting Project, and the Cyprus Investigative Reporting Network - as well as the Bureau of Investigative Journalism - have been reporting on the leaked files since 2023 as part of the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists' Cyprus Confidential investigation. In 2022, Panorama also reported on how Abramovich had made his fortune from a corrupt deal to buy a Russian state-owned oil company in the 1990s, selling it back to the government a decade later for billions in profit. He has previously said allegations of corruption in the deal are false. The profits from Abramovich's oil deals in Russia were funnelled into a web of offshore companies. They were administered from Cyprus by a corporate services firm called MeritServus, in Limassol, the island's second-largest city. Until 2005, Deloitte - now the biggest of the "big four" firms which dominate the accounting industry - owned MeritServus. After they split, the two companies worked closely together with Abramovich's associates to manage his global fortune. The leaked documents from MeritServus reveal some of their practices. Our first example of backdated paperwork comes in 2006, after a new law in Cyprus meant that company accounts had to be made public. The new transparency law threatened to expose the secrets of Abramovich's vast wealth. Deloitte Cyprus had prepared draft accounts for 2003 - but had not yet finalised them - for his Cypriot company Amiscan Investments. The accounts detailed $672m of luxury property. A mansion in West Sussex, a luxury flat in London and an estate in the south of France were all included - plus helicopters, private jets and a small fleet of boats the oligarch owned at the time, including the $147.5m Pelorus. To keep them secret, Abramovich's associates and Meritservus decided to rewrite history. They drew up a plan to circumvent the transparency law by transferring the assets to Amiscan's parent company in the British Virgin Islands (BVI), where they could be kept hidden. And they backdated the change by three years to make it look like the asset transfer had happened in 2003. Deloitte Cyprus reviewed the backdated documents and said they were "adequate" to allow them to remove the assets from Amiscan's accounts. When the 2003 accounts were signed off by Deloitte in 2006, the homes, planes and yachts disappeared at the stroke of a pen. Only $75,000 of assets remained. Deloitte signed off the accounts even though the leaked documents show it knew they were completely misleading. Lord Sikka, professor of accounting at the University of Sheffield, said it was a "violation of a statutory duty" and "pretty scandalous" to misrepresent transaction dates and not to publish true and fair accounts. Panorama also found evidence that backdated documents had been used in a tax evasion scheme. This involved another one of Abramovich's Cypriot companies, Kravin Investments, which had almost $2bn in the bank in 2003. It had been earning large amounts in interest, so Roman Abramovich's company should have been paying tax on that interest to the Cypriot authorities. But his advisers had another idea to rewrite history. An email from MeritServus in August 2005 to Abramovich's Russian associates said a plan had been devised after a meeting with Deloitte. "If you agree, it will be necessary to change the financial statements and the accounting records accordingly for 2003 and 2004," the email read. MeritServus informed the oligarch's Russian associates, that Kravin's "Provisional Tax Assessments for 2005" would be filed showing the company earning no income from the money. A month later, an associate in Russia emailed in response, "I agree". MeritServus then created a series of backdated documents which falsely purported to show that Kravin was only holding and investing the funds on behalf of its parent company in the BVI. This made it look like Kravin did not actually own the money, so it would not be liable for tax in Cyprus. Deloitte wrote in a September 2005 email that "certain changes will have to be made to the accounts (bank account balances, interest income, profit and loss account)" because of the backdated changes to Kravin's assets. So Deloitte was apparently advising on the falsification of financial records. The evidence suggests it allowed Abramovich's company to evade millions in tax. Andrew Mitchell KC told us the scheme was "straightforward" tax evasion. "If it happened in England and it was in the millions, His Majesty's Revenue and Customs would be thinking about a prosecution," he said. Cypriot MP Christos Christofides said that if tax had been evaded, then "we have to see how we can get our money back and how, if some people are guilty, they have to pay the price according to our law." In addition to the documents which Deloitte helped to backdate, Abramovich's advisers at MeritServus falsified a third set of records. This involved the oligarch's huge business fortune - more than $10bn - held by a company called Electus Investments in Cyprus. MeritServus backdated documents to make it look like Electus did not own the fortune. It used another Abramovich company with exactly the same name of Electus Investments, but this time based in the more secretive BVI, where accounts did not have to be made public. Emails show that in 2006, MeritServus acknowledged that the fortune was owned by Electus Cyprus. But again it proposed to rewrite the past, this time "to transfer the beneficial ownership to Electus Investments in the BVI" and make it look as though the change had happened three years earlier. MeritServus signed and backdated documents which falsely purported to show the BVI company had owned the $10bn fortune since 20 November 2003. So when the accounts of the Cypriot company with the same name were made public, it appeared to have assets worth just $145,000. Roman Abramovich's billions had been made to disappear. Andrew Mitchell KC told Panorama: "What you take away from it is there are professionals who are prepared to bend and break the rules of their profession and therefore the law. And it looks that they will stop literally at nothing in terms of creating documents." Vladimir Milov, Russia's deputy minister of energy as Abramovich built his empire and now a critic of the Russian government, said: "For each Russian oligarch or Middle Eastern or African corrupt oligarch, there's an army of Western financial and legal services and PR services providers, who is easily taking money for whitewashing their reputation and making them look normal." Denying any wrongdoing by the oligarch, Roman Abramovich's lawyers said that he was "not involved in the day-to-day operation of those companies" and that where arrangements were proposed by professional advisers, "reliance on that advice was entirely proper and legitimate". Deloitte Cyprus said it could not comment on the specific allegations because the documents were more than 20 years old and no longer accessible. title: Dozens of gold prospectors killed in strikes on Egypt-Sudan border, rights group says
content: At least 72 civilians who had been prospecting for gold in a border region of Sudan have been killed in air strikes, a regional rights group says. Emergency Lawyers, based in the Sudanese capital, Khartoum, said jets targeted the so-called artisanal miners at a popular gold mining sites in Sudan's River Nile state on Saturday. Neither the Egyptian government nor the de facto Sudanese authorities have so far commented. Cairo has previously faced accusations of deadly strikes on gold prospectors as part of a crackdown on illicit activity along its southern border. Emergency Lawyers noted the previous alleged attacks and said they represented not only a violation of Sudan's sovereign territory but demonstrated the government's lack of control over the region. "The deliberate targeting of unarmed civilians violates international humanitarian law and the right to life," it said in a statement on Sunday. "These acts may constitute war crimes." It noted that its death toll was provisional and could rise. The Paris-based Sudan Tribune reported that the death toll could far exceed the number reported by Emergency Lawyers, citing a survivor of Saturday's attack who said many more people had been injured. Eyewitnesses said the attack began around 06:00 local time (04:00 GMT), with the aircraft firing more than five missiles directly at the miners' camps, destroying them and excavation pits with people still inside, the newspaper wrote. The Sudan Tribune reported claims in June that Egyptian forces had used drones and artillery to target artisanal mining sites in the same region, killing several, after sporadic incidents of Egyptian border guards of burning equipment, torching temporary shelters, and firing live ammunition to disperse mine workers. Days later, Egypt's border agency announced that it and the military had begun a sweeping security campaign along the border to foil illegal migration, drug smuggling and illegal mining. At the same time, Sudan's de facto leader announced an investigation into the alleged strikes, which were said to have killed dozens. Gold lies at the core of the border tensions. Sudan's ongoing civil war has led to a surge in artisanal mining - an often risky practice conducted by civilians with rudimentary tools and without official permission - particularly in remote areas near its borders. Gold-rich areas such as those in River Nile state lie along porous borders in terrain historically associated with cross-border smuggling routes, with artisanally mined gold potentially feeding into those channels. Egypt's border force said in June that it had seized 86 tonnes of gold ore along with amateur prospecting equipment. Artisanal mining has also reportedly continued in Sudan's conflict zones and smuggled gold may be a source of income for armed insurgent groups. This has raised concerns of illicit Sudanese gold undermining the legitimate Egyptian gold market. After analysing 1,500 videos and images of the Raila Odinga memorial, Africa Eye finds that those killed were far from the scuffles. The boat was travelling from Djibouti to Yemen with 305 people on board, when it capsized near the port town of Obock on Thursday night. Fresh details reveal how the 40-year-old businessman flew and crossed regional borders while seriously ill. Pillay is recognised for her "efforts to promote peace and international law", the Norwegian Nobel Committee says. title: Children among 139 dead after boat capsizes off Djibouti, UN says
content: At least 139 migrants including 15 children have died and dozens more are still missing after a boat sank off the coast of Djibouti, the UN's migration office has said. The boat had been travelling from Djibouti to Yemen with 305 people aboard when it capsized near the port town of Obock on Thursday night. Around 82 people were rescued, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said. IOM's Djibouti mission chief Alexandre Coissac called the tragedy a "stark reminder" of the dangers migrants face when seeking a new life elsewhere. Tens of thousands of migrants from the Horn of Africa make the perilous journey each year hoping to reach Gulf countries for safety and work, the agency says. The organisation revised its toll from 109 on Sunday after 30 more bodies were recovered. "This is a devastating loss of life," Coissac said. "Our thoughts are with the survivors and the families who have lost loved ones or remain without news of their relatives." Local authorities are also arranging burials for those who have died, while the survivors - all Ethiopian nationals - have medical care readily available to them. Yemen remains engulfed in a devastating civil war that has lasted more than a decade. Despite this conflict - and growing instability across the wider region - migrants still cross the Bab el-Mandeb Strait to Yemen driven by poverty, insecurity and the growing impacts of climate change. Since 10 September, the IOM said its Displacement Tracking Matrix had observed more than 20,000 "movements" from Ethiopia to Djibouti. IOM said it was providing assistance to 64 of the survivors at its response centre in Obock, including healthcare and support to "restore contact with their families". The UN agency was working in "close collaboration" with local authorities to help migrants and "prevent deaths at sea and on land", it added. More than 900 migrants died or went missing taking the same route in 2025, during an 18% increase in the number of people attempting the journey, according to IOM statistics. In March 2026, nine people were killed and 45 went missing following a similar incident as Thursday's. The conflict in Yemen has also displaced more than 130,000 people across the country, the UN refugee agency said last month. Thousands of Yemenis have fled to Djibouti to escape the civil war between Houthi fighters and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government. Djibouti is a tiny former French colony that sits just across the Gulf of Aden from Yemen. After analysing 1,500 videos and images of the Raila Odinga memorial, Africa Eye finds that those killed were far from the scuffles. The Saudi capital has been hit by multiple attacks from the Iran-backed Yemeni group over the weekend. All asylum applications would be rejected and existing ones voided, with all claimants marked for deportation. Neither Egypt nor Sudan has commented on the alleged strikes on an artisanal mining camp on Saturday. While the physical damage from Houthi attacks can be quickly repaired, the Saudi reputation for stability is taking a battering. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: Could Alberta's vote on independence be Canada's Brexit moment?
content: People in the province of Alberta will vote on 19 October on whether they want to start the process of separating from the rest of Canada. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has called the upcoming referendum a "dangerous bluff", comparing it to the Brexit vote that saw the UK leave the European Union. But supporters of Albertan independence believe that the oil-rich province has long been overlooked by decision-makers in Ottawa, the national capital, and that federal environmental policies have hindered its ability to develop its natural resources. So, could Alberta really become its own country? The BBC's Nadine Yousif takes us on a journey through Alberta to talk to both supporters and opponents of separation about their hopes for the country's future. Video by Eloise Alanna. The BBC's Nada Tawfik goes through new dramatic body cam footage that shows the tense moments when police arrive on scene. Protests against sexual violence took place across more than 40 US states on 8 October. Isaias will bring damaging winds, torrential rain and a storm surge with landfall expected late Friday. The BBC's Madeline Gerber describes the conditions of the mansion where the children - some as young as two months old - were living. The US death row inmate's legal team said at a press conference that she is now "conscious and speaking" after her failed execution. The BBC's Sarah Smith details the injuries sustained by the US death row inmate after two failed lethal injections, and what comes next. The BBC's Samira Hussain explains the impact the $110bn merger will have on consumers of both entertainment giants. The White House said Trump was warning of the risk a nuclear Iran with his comments at a Nebraska rally. The Pentagon confirmed on Sunday it had removed its bombers - thought to be about a dozen B-1s - from the base back to their home stations in America. The bodycam footage also shows a police officer finding a gun in Mangione's backpack, days after the killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson. title: Mourners killed by Kenya police at ex-PM's national farewell not part of violence, BBC finds
content: Three mourners killed when Kenyan police opened fire at a national farewell for former Prime Minister Raila Odinga were not involved in a clash that sparked gunfire, a BBC Africa Eye investigation has found. During an event held last October for people to pay their respects to Odinga, three people were shot dead after mourners attempted to gain access to the VIP section of Nairobi's Kasarani Stadium by force. BBC analysis from inside the stadium shows the victims were each between at least 60m (197 ft) and 160m from the scuffles. Kenya's Interior Minister Kipchumba Murkomen told the BBC that the police action had been "restrained" after the crowd starting throwing stones. In footage analysed by the BBC, it is clear that objects, including plastic chairs, are thrown, but we have no evidence that they included stones. The BBC went through more than 1,500 images and videos to establish the location of those killed in the stadium on 16 October 2025, and also spoke to some of their relatives. Forensic analysis by the BBC suggests an elite police unit responsible for protecting the president may have fired the fatal shots. Kenya's longest serving opposition leader and former prime minister died the previous day while receiving medical treatment in India. He was one of the country's most influential political figures. A year on, Kenya's police watchdog, the Independent Policing Oversight Authority (IPOA), is still investigating the deaths and police response and no-one has been held to account. The interior minister defended the police by saying they had been under "so much pressure" after working for many hours non-stop and had been deployed to a new venue at the last minute. "The investigations are being done by an independent police oversight authority, we believe that their findings will help us take appropriate legal action," Murkomen said. Responding to questions about the conduct of police he said: "I don't think… somebody [was] sitting there and saying: 'Shoot now'. It is the judgment of the police officer at the spur of the moment." Yvonne Akinyi, who husband was among those killed told the BBC: "The people who we look at to protect us, these are the people that cause us this pain. These are the people that make us to become young widows in this country, young orphans in this county," she said. Odinga's death at 80 prompted an outpouring of grief across Kenya. Thousands gathered at Nairobi's Jomo Kenyatta International Airport as his body was flown home. The body had originally been due to lie in state at parliament, but the scale of the crowds and fears of a security breach forced a last-minute change of venue to Kasarani Stadium. Officials say they had little time to secure the 48,000-capacity venue, and thousands spilled onto the pitch and into the stands unchecked. After several hours of waiting to see the coffin in 30C heat with no public address system for official updates, a small section of the crowd began throwing objects, including plastic chairs, at officers guarding the VIP pavilion. Police fired live rounds as mourners pushed toward the pavilion. Footage from elsewhere in the stadium shows the crowd remained largely peaceful. In total, three people were killed. One of them was Evans Kiche, a 40 year-old-chef and father to seven children. BBC analysis shows he was around 60m from the confrontation when he was killed by a gunshot wound to the head. The two other mourners killed, Vincent Ogutu and Jidah Burka, were at least 160m away, in the opposite stands, far removed from the pavilion. Autopsy reports confirm that Ogutu died from a gunshot wound to the chest and 42 year-old Burka was fatally shot in the head. Piecing together a timeline of events, BBC Africa Eye identified at least eight police officers operating together, wearing tactical clothing and military camouflage. These officers carry assault rifles, with no visible insignia and faces covered. Their uniforms and movements are consistent with a layer of security assigned to President William Ruto and other VIPs before and after the shooting. At least three officers of this unit appear to fire their weapons. The BBC identified three of them as part of an elite police unit responsible for presidential protection. The BBC cannot establish which bullets killed each victim, and cannot rule out other officers firing inside the stadium. Kenya's National Police Service told the BBC: "There are huge lessons picked from the day's events," which had "formed a fundamental learning curve for a better, more professional application in the future." The IPOA did not respond to a request for comment. Ogutu, a 36-year-old father of three, hadn't planned to go to Kasarani, his wife told the BBC. He was in central Nairobi on the morning of 16 October with friends when they saw the crowds heading to the stadium and decided to join. Within hours, he was dead. His widow Yvonne Akinyi described how the killing upended their family, saying their children were now orphans. As she prepares to mark a year since her husband's death, Akinyi is no closer to understanding why he died while paying his respects at an event organised by the government. "I will just try to be that strong woman. Very strong. But deep inside there is a hole," she said. "It is very painful because sometimes you just sit down and ask yourself. At Kasarani there were so many people, so many of them. Why him." Go to BBCAfrica.com for more news from the African continent. title: Wildlife park remains closed after tiger attack
content: Yorkshire Wildlife Park remains closed after a man climbed into a tiger enclosure and was fatally attacked by the animal. Emergency services were called to the park near Doncaster, South Yorkshire, at about 13:30 BST on Saturday after reports of a man climbing down into the enclosure from a walkway. An eyewitness described seeing the man wearing headphones and "pacing around" near the enclosure before he went in and was attacked. Police said the man sadly died at the scene. A park spokesperson said their "thoughts and heartfelt sympathies" remain with the man's family and confirmed the Amur tiger, called Altai, remained in the enclosure and would not be euthanised. The spokesperson says many people had contacted them about the tiger and he was safe and well. Staff who were at the scene who were "deeply affected by events" would receive specialist support, they added. South Yorkshire Police said the man's family were being supported by officers. "Our thoughts are with them at this distressing time," the force said in a statement. It added: "We are aware of videos circulating online and we would encourage people not to share this footage." Earlier on Saturday, in a statement posted on its website, the park said its emergency response procedures had been "immediately activated" and it was "working closely with the authorities to ascertain exactly what happened". Ella Ford, 24, from Moreton, Wirral, had visited the park with her boyfriend and filmed the tiger moments before the attack. She described seeing a man by the tiger enclosure "pacing around with his headphones in". A few minutes later, she saw the same man had "climbed up onto the barriers". A woman was close by talking to him, she said, before "he jumped in and crawled in front of the tiger, where the tiger was perched and just lay there". Ford said she then witnessed the tiger grab hold of the man, who she reported as "shouting for help". She estimates around 15 to 20 people were on the enclosure's raised visitor walkway before staff quickly evacuated the area, and shortly afterwards, the park. She described members of the public as being "confused, like what on earth's going on?" "I just know some man was obviously trying to bang on the fence to try and deter the tiger away, but it obviously wasn't doing anything," she said. Karmelle Pelham, 39, from Worksop, had been enjoying a family day out when park staff told them the site was being evacuated. She said she had heard what sounded like "gunshots" and an air ambulance had circled above. Pelham added: "There was a big, black tarpaulin over the tiger enclosure." She praised park staff for their handling of the incident, saying it had been "very, very well organised". Foreign Secretary and MP for Doncaster North Ed Miliband said he was "deeply saddened" to hear of the incident and sent his "thoughts and deepest condolences to the family of the individual who died." He added he was "very grateful to the emergency services and staff of the park who responded." Lee Pitcher, MP for Doncaster East and the Isle of Axholme, expressed his gratitude to emergency services for their response. In a statement shared to social media, he said he was "deeply saddened to hear about the tragic incident that has taken place at Yorkshire Wildlife Park today". Yorkshire Wildlife Park opened in 2009, with its Land of the Tigers area opening in 2011. The purpose-built two-acre reserve is home to Amur tigers, an endangered subspecies with around 500 left in the wild. Photos of the enclosure on the park's website shows a high walkway for visitors and fencing above the section where the tigers can roam. title: Robert Pattinson on new film Primetime and how hunting predators became hit TV
content: Robert Pattinson is having quite the year. The British actor has already starred opposite Zendaya in The Drama, and played a key role in summer blockbuster The Odyssey. But his new film, Primetime, takes him in a completely new direction - as he portrays the real-life host of American TV show, To Catch a Predator. The show, which aired from 2004 to 2007, involved hunting alleged child abusers. For Pattinson, who became a father almost three years ago, the film's plot is particularly concerning. "It's both the most terrifying thing that can happen to you, whether you're a parent, or even if you're not," he told BBC News at the film's screening at London Film Festival. "It's the most unimaginable sin possible," he added. The new A24 crime thriller depicts the show's host, NBC journalist Chris Hansen, carrying out sting operations on would-be predators. The show was a ratings hit. But it also led to questions over where to draw the line between investigative journalism, police activity and reality television. Speaking on Sunday night, Pattinson reflected on the show's complicated legacy. "The show was this kind of microcosm of saying, 'oh, we can do something about [child abuse], and we can do something about it really, really, really quickly," he said. "And in some ways, that's correct, but it also makes for incredibly powerful TV, and that's when it gets into slightly dicey territory." When asked whether he thinks attitudes towards entertainment have now changed, Pattinson paused. "I think on mainstream TV, but then it's just been replaced," he replied, pointing out that similar content has since appeared on social media. "That's why I was interested in the show, because I could see the beginning of a new wave of 'predator catching' in pretty much the same format that it was in the early 2000s," he said. "And I was just interested as to why that was happening." "And it got bigger and bigger and bigger, and now it's one of the most massive things on social media." Hansen himself has been critical of the film, calling it "bizarre" and "detached from reality" in a video posted on X . Addressing his criticisms, director Lance Oppenheim said: "I agree, that was by design. "I always thought of this movie as more of a fever dream than something that was representational portrait." Oppenheim added there was something "ancient" about the desire to watch people getting publicly punished. "It's happened for thousands of years," he added. "I wanted to make something that interrogated that." Oppenheim, who is also currently co-directing with Nathan Fielder a highly anticipated documentary about Elizabeth Holmes, said separately of that project: "I want everyone to see it. It's a really special movie." Pattinson, 40, became something of a pin-up after playing vampire Edward Cullen in the Twilight series, alongside American actress Kristen Stewart. Before that, he stole young hearts as Hufflepuff hunk Cedric Diggory in Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire. He has since starred in major films including Christopher Nolan's Tenet, as well as a range of eccentric, indie films. This year, he has been on a roll, with Dune: Part Three still to come. He’s also got the next Batman film in the pipeline, although production on that has reportedly paused . When asked when they'll be back to work, Pattinson didn’t give much away ("We don't know yet, but yeah, working on it.") Primetime has also led to speculation that this could be the year that Pattinson gets his first ever Oscars nomination. Is that likely, I wonder? "I am eternally grateful that I got these jobs," he responds. "But then [to have] been able to even do them, this is one of the best years of my life." The Borat star said he was "beyond delighted" to be working on the show, The Popinjay Cavalier, with the Pulp Fiction director. Walters, best known for playing Gwen West in the BBC comedy, was partnered with professional Aljaz Skorjanec. Rupert Harold says the rags to riches film was shot across Europe and Norfolk. title: Pope Leo to have surgery after lump found on lung
content: Pope Leo XIV has announced he will be operated on "in the coming days" after a nodule was found on his lung during a medical check-up. "The doctors found an early, well-localised nodule on my lung," he told the public during his weekly Sunday prayers in St Peter's Square in Rome. The 71-year-old said his medical team "believe it would be right to intervene" and he had agreed to the operation, while reassuring pilgrims that the mass was "well-contained" and caught "at an early stage". The pontiff's admission that he would need surgery comes nearly a year-and-a-half after he succeeded the late Pope Francis, who also experienced issues with his lungs that required hospital treatment. Leo concluded his Angelus prayer by thanking everyone for their "spiritual closeness" and said he entrusted himself to their prayers. Holy See Press Office spokesman Matteo Bruni told the media that "the operation is scheduled for the first days of next week". He added that the Pope is expected to take about a week to recover. Vatican News, the Holy See's news portal, said the operation will take place at Gemelli Hospital in Rome. The hospital set up a special Papal suite following the failed assassination attempt on Pope John Paul II's life in May 1981, which is still in use today. Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni expressed her "personal solidarity" with the Pope as he "faces the ordeal ahead in the coming days". Her sentiments were echoed by Italian President Sergio Mattarella, who offered his "sincerest wishes for a peaceful recovery and a speedy and full return to health". Isaac Herzog, the president of Israel, also wished the pontiff "a full and speedy recovery". The Pope, born Robert Francis Prevost, is the 267th occupant of the throne of St Peter – the first US citizen to do so. He was ordained in 1982 and spent years as a missionary in Peru, where he is remembered as a figure who worked with marginalised communities. During Sunday's service, the Pope confirmed his upcoming visit to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru in November will still go ahead. The Archbishop of Montevideo, Daniel Sturla, said preparations for his tour will continue with "greater enthusiasm" as he called for prayers for his recovery. A lung nodule is a small lump of tissue that is usually detected following an X-ray or CT scan of the chest, according to the NHS. Most nodules do not cause other symptoms. The Rt Rev Menezes moves from his role within the Catholic church in Birmingham. Archbishop William Nolan said the move to close 24 churches was forced by "too many parishes but too few people". The former Bishop of Broome is one of the most senior Catholic clerics in the world to face sex abuse charges. title: Teen 'detached from reality' to cope with return of aggressive cancer
content: A teenage boy with lymphoma says he coped with the return of his cancer by detaching himself from his illness, following advice from father who also faced the disease. Ethan Griffiths, 14, was diagnosed with Burkitt lymphoma - a type of fast-growing non-Hodgkin lymphoma (nHL) - in January, undergoing chemotherapy and being declared cancer-free in May, before having an "aggressive" relapse . The sport and gaming-mad teen, who underwent a new treatment being trialled in Bristol, came home to Maesteg cancer-free again in September. "Through it all I tried to stay as positive as I could," said Ethan, adding it was his dad Lloyd, also a cancer survivor, who was often "losing his head". News of the young rugby player's relapse came just two weeks after getting home from the hospital. "It was much more heartbreaking because I was getting back into everything," he said. "I went to school for half a day, and I was going to the gym quite regularly and getting back into fitness. "Then obviously to hear that news was really horrendous." His family faced "immeasurable stress" as Ethan joined a clinical trial at Bristol Royal Hospital Children for patients with B-cell nHL who had not responded to treatment or had relapsed. The UK-wide trial involving two new drugs offered just a 50% chance of success. "I would just switch off and he'd be losing his head next to me," Ethan said, nodding to his dad. His strategy for staying calm was simple: "Stick my earphones in, listen to music and try to fall asleep." Lloyd admitted his son probably got his "stoic side" from mum Rusanne. But the 56-year-old project manager said his own experience with a different type of lymphoma may have also helped. He said: "One thing I said to Ethan from the start, probably when we first found out he'd relapsed, was: 'You're a passenger on this journey. You're not in control, you can't affect the outcome. So you have to kind of keep trying to detach yourself'." Lloyd said Ethan "seemed to detach himself entirely from this whole nine months in a way". "It's been quite inspiring really, how well he's managed to do that." Ethan said in some ways undergoing treatment a second time was easier because he knew what to expect. But mentally he said it was harder. "Obviously you are thinking to yourself 'When is this all going to end?'" His latest treatment involved intensive chemotherapy followed by a transplant using stem cells collected earlier in the process. It meant spending several weeks in hospital in protective isolation. "I found it alright to be honest," Ethan said. "It was just very boring because we were in isolation." Now home, Ethan is trying to get back to normal life. He said he still becomes "really tired just walking" and knows it will take time to get back to rugby. His immediate priority is to "build things up slowly with fitness" and catch up on schoolwork, initially through online lessons before gradually returning to the classroom. "When my health is back up, start going in for half days maybe and slowly build everything back up," Ethan said.
